messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cybersecurity Analyst
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tran Minh Duc is a 75-year-old Vietnamese American man, widowed, who works part-time as a cybersecurity analyst from his home in the suburbs of San Jose. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 74, reflecting severe and pervasive posttraumatic stress symptoms following an event that occurred more than four decades ago but which, in his own words, "never stopped happening."

When Duc was in his early thirties, his youngest son, Khoi, then eighteen months old, developed bacterial meningitis. The illness progressed with terrifying speed. Within hours of Duc noticing the child's stiff neck and unusual cry, Khoi was admitted to the intensive care unit, where medical staff performed a lumbar puncture while Duc was made to wait outside a curtained bay. He remembers the antiseptic smell of the ward with extraordinary precision — a sharp, chemical odour that seemed to saturate his clothes, his hair, his skin. He remembers a nurse carrying a newborn past him in the corridor as he waited, the sight of that healthy infant making the contrast with his own child almost unbearable. He remembers the way a physician placed a hand on his shoulder and spoke slowly, and how Duc understood from the cadence of the words before he understood their content that his son might not survive the night. Khoi did survive, though he sustained partial hearing loss. Duc has never fully absorbed that outcome as real.

In the months after Khoi's hospitalisation, Duc found himself returning compulsively to the hours of that night. The memory did not behave like ordinary recollection. It arrived unbidden and played in its entirety — the fluorescent corridor, the smell, the nurse with the newborn, the physician's measured voice — as though it were footage on a loop that he had no means of stopping. More disorienting still was the quality of presentness the memory carried. When it came, Duc did not feel that he was remembering something that had ended; he felt that it was still occurring, that Khoi was still behind that curtain, that the outcome was still undecided. He had come to believe that there was something fundamentally wrong with his mind, that a healthy person would simply know the difference between then and now.

Over the years his wife, Linh, had been the person who helped him navigate around the sharpest edges of his daily life. After her death three years ago, those edges became unavoidable. His work in cybersecurity, which he conducts remotely, requires occasional in-person consultations at client offices, and one such client is a large hospital system. The first time Duc walked into that building to review their network security protocols, the antiseptic smell hit him before he had crossed the lobby threshold. His heart rate surged, his hands began to tremble, and he stood frozen for nearly a minute before a colleague guided him to a chair. He has since declined every in-person visit to that client, offering technical justifications that have begun to strain his professional relationships. His supervisor has noted his reluctance in writing.

Outside work, Duc avoids his son Khoi's neighbourhood, where a maternity clinic recently opened. He changes his route to the pharmacy to bypass it. When a colleague's pregnancy was announced in a video call and someone held up a scan image to the camera, Duc left the call without explanation. He has not been able to explain this to colleagues or to Khoi, in part because when he attempts to tell the story of that night, something fractures in the telling. He loses the sequence, trails into silence, and cannot find his way back to a conclusion. He has come to dread being asked about it, and so he offers nothing.

What finally brought Duc to seek help was a routine cardiology appointment last month. The examination room smelled exactly as that hospital ward had smelled. He experienced a flashback of such intensity that the cardiologist paused the examination and asked whether he was all right. Duc was not able to answer. He sat in his car for an hour afterward before he could drive. He made a therapy referral the following week. What he is most afraid of is that the memory will never be something that belongs to the past. What he most hopes for, quietly and with some difficulty articulating it, is to be present with his son without being somewhere else at the same time.
